analysis.one_liner: Requires freight railroads to provide shippers timely, reliable service and lets regulators enforce it quickly.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since it was introduced in June 2025, with no hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require freight railroads to serve shippers in a way that meets their need for timely, efficient, and reliable rail service. It would tell the Surface Transportation Board — the federal agency overseeing railroads — to consider things like crew availability, employee reductions, and equipment maintenance when deciding whether a railroad has failed to provide required service. It would also speed up complaints: service-violation cases would have to be decided within 180 days, and requests for service terms within 45 days, with the Board empowered to order specific delivery times and standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that ship freight by rail — farmers, manufacturers, and retailers — gain a legally enforceable right to reliable, on-time rail service with fast government review of complaints. Consumers benefit indirectly through steadier supply chains and fewer shortages and price spikes caused by rail service failures. Rail workers gain because employee reductions and crew availability must be weighed when carriers are judged on service.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail shippers, rail workers, and consumers

how_it_helps.text: It requires railroads to provide service that meets each shipper's need for timely, efficient, and reliable rail transportation, and to honor reasonable requested service requirements.

It directs the Surface Transportation Board to consider crew availability, employee reductions, equipment maintenance, and local service schedules when deciding whether a carrier has failed to provide required service.
It requires the Board to expedite service-violation cases — completed within 180 days — and service-term cases within 45 days, instead of letting them drag on.
If a carrier is found to have failed to provide required service, the Board must set reasonable transit or cycle times and other service standards to fix the problem.

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads would bear the cost of meeting enforceable service standards — maintaining crews, equipment, and schedules they might otherwise cut to save money — and of expedited regulatory proceedings. Some of those costs could be passed through in shipping rates.

drawbacks.text: Railroads would face new, enforceable federal service standards, with regulators empowered to dictate transit and cycle times and to force staffing- and equipment-related changes — compliance could be costly for carriers.

Requiring the Board to weigh crew and employee reductions when judging service violations could constrain the precision scheduled railroading practices that made railroads more profitable, an approach railroads argue can raise costs and reduce network flexibility.
The bill has not received any committee action, so there has been no opportunity for hearings or amendments to test whether the standards it sets are workable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is faster, more reliable rail service for shippers, which translates into steadier supply chains and fewer price and availability problems for consumers, plus enforceable service standards and expedited cases so complaints are not tied up for years. The costs are real: railroads could face meaningful compliance expenses, and there is a fair concern that rigid service mandates and crew-related rules could reduce the operating flexibility railroads say keeps the network efficient, possibly raising shipping prices. On balance the bill targets a documented service-reliability problem and gives the regulator tools to fix it, but it has not been examined or amended in committee, so its workability is untested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the Reliable Rail Service Act of 2025 in the Senate on June 18, 2025, with Sen. Roger Marshall as a Republican cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action has been taken: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Freight railroads are better off so far — with no action in committee, they face no new enforceable service standards, while shippers waiting for reliability get nothing.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to hold freight railroads accountable for reliable service to shippers.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican to sign on.

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Holds the bill; it has taken no action since the bill was referred on June 18, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a bipartisan sponsor pair — a Wisconsin Democrat and a Kansas Republican — but with only one Republican cosponsor among 55, no vote has occurred to show how the chambers would split.

industries.note: The bill would make railroads legally accountable for service quality, allowing the Surface Transportation Board to impose binding transit times and weigh staffing and equipment levels in enforcement cases. Railroads would lose the operational flexibility they used after past service failures.

Shippers would get enforceable service standards, faster complaints (180 days), and leverage in negotiating service terms. Better rail service also reduces supply disruptions and costs that get passed on to consumers.

industries.industry: Rail labor (train crews, maintenance, dispatch, customer service employees)
industries.note: The bill requires the Board to consider crew reductions and crew availability when judging carrier service violations, giving railroad employees' working conditions a formal place in service enforcement.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Commerce Committee with no hearing or markup scheduled and only one Republican cosponsor among 55 Senate Republicans. A single-cosponsor bill of this kind would typically need committee action and broader support to reach the floor; without it, the bill is likely to stall in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress.
